Senses.Explanation: Literally ‘grasp or take in hand’ (把) + ‘fix or settle’ (定): to hold fast, keep firmly in hand, or hold in check. The compound has 684 occurrences in 186 allowlisted texts. Its principal corpus contrast is ‘release or let go’ (放行): the contiguous pair ‘hold fast and release’ (把定放行) occurs 15 times in 13 texts. Wansong quotes the saying, ‘when held fast, true gold loses its color; when released, rubble shines’ (把定真金失色，放行瓦礫生光), and the text calls this ‘having capture and release, able to kill and bring to life’ (謂之有擒有縱，能殺能活). Xuedou's record preserves the same opposition: ‘when released, rubble shines; when held fast, true gold loses color; the authority is in hand, killing and bringing to life accord with the occasion’ (放行則瓦礫生光，把定則真金失色，權柄在手，殺活臨時). The common objects show its grammar: ‘hold heaven and earth fast’ (把定乾坤) has 113 occurrences in 60 texts; ‘hold the world fast’ (把定世界) 39 in 31; ‘hold the key crossing’ (把定要津) 29 in 22; and ‘hold the throat’ (把定咽喉) 8 in 8. In a recorded question, Jiufeng is asked ‘what is the eye that holds heaven and earth fast?’ (如何是把定乾坤眼) and answers, ‘heaven and earth are inside it’ (乾坤在裏許), then identifies that as the heaven-and-earth eye (正是乾坤眼). Wansong elsewhere explicitly says one eye ‘is also called the eye that holds heaven and earth fast, continuously leaking not the slightest thread, and is also named the diamond eye at the crown’ (一隻眼又喚作把定乾坤眼，綿綿不漏絲毫，亦名頂門具金剛眼). These are the text's own contrasts and equivalences.
Senses.Note: The corpus uses the same verb for concrete grasping, for holding a passage or throat, and in the paired critical vocabulary ‘hold fast / release’ (把定／放行); these uses retain the literal opposition and do not require separate senses. Wansong further states, ‘where the ancients held fast, they could release and advance from the top of a pole; when releasing, they could hold firm, standing like a thousand-fathom wall’ (古人把定處放得行竿頭進步，放行時把得定壁立千仞). The record thus refuses a simple equation of holding with one fixed outcome; this entry reports the wording without assigning an intent to it.

Occurrences.Kwic: 裂開也在我，揑聚也在我。諸方道：把定真金失色，放行瓦礫生光。謂之有擒有縱，能殺能活。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wansong's commentary on case 14: ‘splitting open is with me; gathering together is with me. Various quarters say: when held fast, true gold loses color; when released, rubble shines. This is called having capture and release, able to kill and bring to life.’ A direct text-drawn contrast and naming formula.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Book of Serenity, raised Jiufeng exchange: a monk asks, ‘what is the eye that holds heaven and earth fast?’ Jiufeng says, ‘heaven and earth are inside it.’ Asked where the eye is, he says, ‘it is precisely the heaven-and-earth eye.’ Raised two-speaker case, so MasterName is null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 乾坤把定不把定。虛空放行不放行。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xudeng lu, Jiangshan Fang section, formal address: ‘heaven and earth—held fast or not held fast; empty space—released or not released.’ The coarse governing head is a lineage group, but the full surrounding text names Jiangshan Fang immediately before the address. He is not roster-linked, so MasterName remains null.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, to take hands and walk together. The phrase occurs 207 times in 105 allowlisted texts. Chan records use it as a verdict of admitted company: a speaker says that whoever can inspect his statement may walk hand in hand south of Mount Sumeru, that one who can seize the snake safely may walk with the old monk, or that one commentator walks with Nanquan. Its companions range from buddhas and patriarchs to named masters and interlocutors who meet the stated test. Yuanwu's case commentary joins the phrase to entering mud and water together, living and dying together, making close participation in a public case—not generic companionship—the phrase's characteristic Chan deployment.
Senses.Note: No distinct referent emerged: literal hand-taking supplies one recurrent metaphorical predicate, applied to different companions. Those companions are deployment variants, not separate senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若點檢得出，須彌南畔把手共行；若點檢不出，布袋裏老鴉雖活如死。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The invitation is conditional on successfully inspecting the speaker's statement.

Occurrences.Kwic: 與他把手共行。他從來有放行手段。敢與爾入泥入水。同死同生。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu expands walking hand in hand as entering mud and water, living and dying together.

Occurrences.Kwic: 於他七寸上。一揑揑住。便與老僧把手共行。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The old monk offers company to one able to seize the snake at its vulnerable point.

Occurrences.Kwic: 雪竇與南泉把手共行。一句說了也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Case commentary says Xuedou walks hand in hand with Nanquan.

Senses.Explanation: Zhuang Zhou is the pre-Chan figure whom the corpus invokes through a small roster of named stories and stock lines, rather than through a general biography. The name occurs 168 times in 93 allowlisted texts. Chan records cite “Zhuang Zhou dreamed of the butterfly; he is not me; the butterfly dreamed of Zhuang Zhou; I am not him” (莊周夢蝶，渠不是我；蝶夢莊周，我不是渠), recount that when his wife died he drummed on a basin and sang, and list learning connected with Confucius, Laozi, Zhuang Zhou, and the Hundred Schools. The corpus also deploys his name in the recurring sword line “Zhuang Zhou’s sword killed three thousand guests; from then on the road to Peach Spring did not go through” (莊周劍殺三千客，從此桃源路不通). A separate teaching-seat formula asks, “where are the three thousand swordsmen now?” and answers, “Zhuang Zhou alone is permitted to bring great peace” (三千劒客今何在？獨許莊周致太平). Another verse directly addresses him: “a message to Zhuang Zhou: stop deliberating” (寄語莊周休擬議). Thus the Zen Zhuang Zhou is the named dreamer, basin-drummer, learned figure, sword-line figure, and addressee that masters quote and redeploy. This entry does not supplement those deployments with an outside life story.
Senses.Note: Dream, mourning story, scholarly reference, sword line, and poetic address all name the same person. They are different deployments, not different referents or readings to split.
